area: Core/Data — readers (HDF5/DM4/EMPAD/MIB), calibration model, LoadSpecification, EMD/Bragg writer and sidecar round trip
summary: This area is genuinely strong on the two things it was designed against. Axis order is NOT casually assumed: every read goes through `LoadView`, which carries source + specification + derived descriptor as one value and re-checks the reader's own discovered shape at every read (`LoadSpecification.swift:428` `requireSource`, called from `H5Reader.swift:474` and each vendor reader), and the py4DSTEM qx/qy ↔ app y/x swap is done exactly once at documented boundaries (`FourDDataSource.swift:46-54`, `Calibration.swift:838-848`, `BraggVectorEMDWriter.swift:2121-2125`). The ellipse transform is a faithful port of `braggvectors.py:504-511` including the `theta - pi/2` convention, and the bin arithmetic reproduces `preprocess.py:181,193` (sum not average, remainder off the END) with the DEVIATION notes the repo rule requires. `CalibrationReReference` is the best file here: crop/bin re-referencing is stated as geometry, refuses rather than clamps, and the pixel-centre bounds test is deliberately written in the positive so NaN cannot pass. Truncated files, overflowing DM4 dims, deep tag nesting, malformed sidecar attributes and newer-schema sidecars all produce named refusals rather than silent wrong arrays. The findings below are all at the edges: a string-type assumption in the sidecar reader that the sibling H5Reader gets right, an asymmetry where results survive a view change but the attribute describing that view does not, and provenance fields that are dropped rather than carried. I found no axis-order defect, no Metal struct issue (out of this area), and no Core/Data code doing UI work. Known items I hit and did not re-report: the HDF5 axis-order lead, `?? .fullExtent` fabricated provenance, the sidecar-frame calibration adoption, the demo fixture's "FCC" comment, and `robustResidual` being dropped by the re-reference.

findings.title: The sidecar reader reads every HDF5 string as variable-length, so a fixed-length string attribute overruns an 8-byte stack slot and then frees a wild pointer
findings.why: `readStringAttribute` (2393-2410) takes the attribute's own file type from `h5agetType` (2400) and passes it straight to `h5aread` with the destination being `&pointer`, a single `UnsafeMutablePointer<CChar>?` — 8 bytes. That is correct ONLY for a variable-length string type. For a fixed-length string of size N, HDF5 writes N bytes there; the code never calls `H5Tis_variable_str` and never sizes a buffer. `String(cString: pointer)` at 2409 then dereferences the first 8 bytes of the string's own content as an address, and the `defer { h5freeMemory(pointer) }` at 2408 frees it. `readStringDataset` (953-971) has the identical shape. This is not an oversight of an unknown technique: the sibling reader `H5Reader.readStringValue` (H5Reader.swift:786-803) does it correctly — it branches on `h5tisVariableStr`, and for the fixed-length case allocates `size + 1` CChars and bounds-checks `size < 4096`. The sidecar format is documented and meant to be interoperable, so a sidecar regenerated from Python (h5py writes fixed-length strings whenever the value is `np.bytes_` rather than `str`) is a realistic input, and these functions are the first thing `loadSession` touches.
findings.failureScenario: A user (or a lab script) writes a `.mac4dstem.h5` sidecar from h5py with `root.attrs['mac4dstem_min_reader_schema'] = np.bytes_('5')` and `root.attrs['mac4dstem_result_nodes'] = np.bytes_('result_strain_1a2b3c4d')`. Opening the source dataset calls `loadSession` → `enforceMinimumReader` → `readStringAttribute`, which passes a 23-byte fixed-length string type to `h5aread` against an 8-byte stack destination: 15 bytes of stack past `pointer` are overwritten, then `String(cString:)` is called on the address formed from the bytes 'result_s'. Result is a crash on open at best; at worst a stack write past the destination plus a free of an attacker-influenced pointer.

findings.title: A saved scalar session result is restored with no shape check, while the RGBA branch three lines below refuses on exactly that mismatch
findings.why: `restoreSessionResult` has two branches. The RGBA branch guards `map.width == descriptor.rx, map.height == descriptor.ry` and refuses with a named status line (2955-2958). The scalar branch (2946-2953) publishes `resultImage`, `restoredResultInfo`, `restoredResultPixelInfo` and `restoredResultDomain` with no comparison against the loaded view at all, then falls through to the shared "Restored <name>" status at 2970. The map's own domain is available one line later — `map.provenance["display_domain"]` — so the correct guard is 'if the restored product is scan-domain, its extent must equal the loaded scan', not the RGBA branch's unconditional one (reconstruction-domain scalars legitimately have their own shape). Neither branch has any test: grepping `mac4DSTEMTests/` and `tools/` for the refusal string returns only the production line. The writer does not close this either — `mergeResultMap` (BraggVectorEMDWriter.swift:535-542) validates the map against ITSELF (`pixels.count == width * height`) and never against the scan it is being saved beside.
findings.failureScenario: A sidecar carries a scan-domain strain map saved from a 64x64 scan crop. The dataset is later opened at a different extent (a different configurator crop, a promote — see the next finding — or the source file regenerated with a 256x256 scan under the same name). `restoreSessionResult` sets `resultImage` to the 64x64 pixels, `restoredResultDomain = .scan`, and the status line reads "Restored Strain ← file.mac4dstem.h5". The viewer presents it as this dataset's scan-domain product, pointer sampling maps screen positions onto a 64x64 grid that no longer corresponds to any scan position in the loaded view, and the map is exportable with this session's provenance keys. The RGBA equivalent (DPC direction, IPF-Z) is refused out loud for the identical mismatch.

findings.title: A full-extent rewrite erases the load-specification attribute while copying the previous view's result nodes forward verbatim, and stamps the file back down to min-reader 5
findings.why: `writeFile` rebuilds the whole sidecar on every save. Existing result nodes are copied forward unconditionally at 1672-1689 (`h5ocopy` per descriptor whose kind differs from the one being replaced) — nothing compares the view those results were computed under with the view being saved. The specification attribute, by contrast, is written only when `loadSpecification` is non-nil AND not full extent (1704-1712), so a full-extent save drops it; and `minimumReaderAttribute` is then written as `minimumReaderSchema(for:)` = 5 (1727-1731, 260-262), stamping the file 'safe for an old reader'. The asymmetry is visible in the same function: the replay record IS preserved when the caller supplies none (`preservedReplayJSON`, 1589-1600) precisely because 'a save that carries none would silently ERASE the recipe'. The specification gets no such preservation, and no check that the preserved results belong to the recorded view. On reopen the missing attribute is read as nil (674-735) and `AppState.swift:2331` turns that into `?? .fullExtent` — the known fabricated-provenance defect, here reached by the writer rather than by an old file.
findings.failureScenario: Crop the scan to 64x64 at (32,32), run strain, Save Session Sidecar (attribute written, min-reader 6). Reconfigure to full extent — the app's headline promote workflow; `CalibrationReReference.apply` returns early at :134-138 with `scanIndexedResultsAreAmbiguous: false`, so nothing warns. Save Session Calibration: `mergeCalibration` is called with `loadedView.specification == .fullExtent`, `writeFile` copies the 64x64 strain node forward, writes no specification attribute, and stamps min-reader 5. Reopening the source now restores a 64x64 crop-frame strain map against the full 256x256 scan (see the previous finding — the scalar branch does not check), with the sidecar asserting it was computed at full extent. This is exactly the 'right numbers at wrong positions, no warning' failure the min-reader marker exists to prevent, produced by the writer that stamps the marker.

findings.title: CalibrationReReference silently drops `excludedFraction`, so a crop or bin converts a trimmed origin fit into one that reports no trim history
findings.why: All three helpers rebuild `OriginMaps` from scratch and pass only `width/height/measuredX/measuredY/fittedX/fittedY`: `cropped` (344-350), `rescaled` (391-397), `shifted` (403-409). `excludedFraction` and `robustResidual` are optional vars, so they default to nil and vanish. `Calibration.swift:556-559` records the drop of `robustResidual` and treats it as harmless once the gate stopped reading it — but `excludedFraction` is still read in three live places and is the owner's explicit 2026-08-28 disclosure decision (`Calibration.swift:408-412`): the readiness detail line (`Calibration.swift:277-283`), the inspector row (`CalibrationDetailsView.swift:64`), and the export provenance keys `origin_fit_excluded_fraction` / `origin_fit_positions_used_fraction` (`ResultExport.swift:438-440`). Worse than losing a label: `originFitRefusal`'s switch (`Calibration.swift:742-753`) reads `.none` as 'these maps carry no trim history at all — imported py4DSTEM origins' and prints no diagnosis, so an in-app robust fit that excluded 22% of the scan is described after a crop as if it had never been trimmed. The comment at 738-740 explicitly warns against exactly this coalescing ('`?? 0` coalesced "never trimmed" into "trimmed and excluded nothing"') — the same conflation is now created upstream by this file.
findings.failureScenario: Fit the origin on a contaminated scan: the robust fit excludes 22% of positions and the readiness row reads "Fit RMS 2.19 px over 78% of positions (22% excluded as outliers)". Reconfigure with a pure detector crop — every residual is bit-identical and nothing is invalidated. The row now reads "Fit RMS 2.19 px" with no scope clause, the inspector's "Positions used" row disappears, and any product exported from this view carries no `origin_fit_excluded_fraction` key. A reader of that export cannot tell the fit used 78% of the scan from one that used all of it.

findings.title: The inspector's excluded-fraction row uses 0.005, the threshold Gate B measured as inside the trim's own false-positive range and replaced with 0.02
findings.why: `Calibration.excludedFractionDisclosureFloor` (Calibration.swift:567) is 0.02, and the comment above it (560-566) records the measurement that set it: 'a 3σ cut on Rayleigh-distributed radial residuals excludes 0.33%–1.08% of positions across σ = 0.1–2.0 px with no outliers planted at all. 2% sits above that whole range. The first version used 0.5%, which is *inside* it, so a perfectly clean scan was told "1% excluded as outliers".' The readiness path (Calibration.swift:277-278) and the refusal path (742-743) both read the constant. The inspector hard-codes `excluded > 0.005` instead — the retired value, verbatim — so the panel still shows the message the measurement was taken to remove. The constant was created to be the single owner of this decision and one of the three call sites does not consult it.
findings.failureScenario: Run Calibrate Origin on a clean scan with σ ≈ 1 px residuals. The robust trim excludes ~0.8% of positions as its own false-positive rate. The Prepare readiness row correctly says nothing (0.008 < 0.02), while the Calibration Details panel displays "Positions used: 99% (1% excluded as outliers)" — telling the user their scan has outliers it does not have, and putting two different claims about one fit on screen at once, which is the #46 label-contradicts-data class this constant was introduced to close.

findings.title: The DM4 parser traps on `Int(UInt64)` for corrupt SPECIAL fields — the guard written for that case sits after the trapping conversion, and the robustness harness's 'no Int trap' claim does not reach it
findings.why: `readDataTag` does `let ninfo = Int(reader.special(dmVersion))` at :319 and only then `guard ninfo >= 0, ninfo <= 4096 else { throw .truncated }` at :321 — a guard whose comment says it exists so 'malformed counts would otherwise drive a huge allocation'. `reader.special` returns a raw `UInt64` read from the file (:518-520), and `Int.init(UInt64)` traps on any value above `Int.max`, so the guard can never see a high-bit-set count: the process dies first. The same unchecked conversion appears at :298 (`nTags`, with no guard at all), :336, :340, :349, :352 and :358 (`length`, which then feeds `nbytes = length * elemSize`). `Int(Double)` at :452 and :459 traps the same way on a NaN/infinite tag value, reachable because `ByteReader.value` decodes encType 6/7 from raw bit patterns (:543-544). This contradicts the file's own stated contract at :495-497: 'BOUNDS: every load is clamp-safe. Reads past the end return 0 and set `overran`, which the parser checks … to throw `.truncated` instead of crashing on malformed/truncated files.' That holds for TRUNCATION (short reads yield 0) but not for CORRUPTION. `tools/dm4-robustness-test/main.swift:198-215` is named `testOverflowDims` and asserts 'no Int trap', but it plants dims of 2^20 as int32 tags — values that convert fine — so it passes while the conversion class it names is untested.
findings.failureScenario: A DM4 with a single flipped byte in a tag's `ninfo` SPECIAL field (or any partially-corrupt DM4 from a failed acquisition or a bad transfer) gives `special()` a value ≥ 2^63. `Int(...)` at :319 raises 'Fatal error: Not enough bits to represent the passed value' and the app terminates on open, with no error dialog and no crash-report-worthy diagnosis, instead of the `DM4Error.truncated` refusal the next line was written to produce.

findings.title: DM4 scan shape and voltage are picked from an unordered Dictionary, so a multi-image DM file can reshape a 3D cube differently on different runs
findings.why: `scanShape(_ needle:)` is `for (key, value) in numbers where key.contains(needle) { return Int(value) }` — it returns the FIRST match in Swift `Dictionary` iteration order, which is unspecified and varies between processes because of per-process hash seeding. Its two results become `shape = [scanY, scanX, dims[1], dims[0]]` for the rank-3 path at :409, i.e. they decide how a flat frame series is folded into a scan grid. `extractCalibration`'s voltage loop at :475-477 has the same shape. The substring match is unanchored, so any tag path containing 'Scan shape X' anywhere in the tree matches — and DM files routinely carry several ImageList entries, each with its own tag subtree. Nothing downstream can catch a wrong-but-plausible fold: `locateDatacube`'s only sanity check is `ry*rx*qy*qx*elementSize == array.bytes` (:422-431), which 32x64 and 64x32 both satisfy identically.
findings.failureScenario: A DM4 holding a survey image alongside the 4D acquisition, where the tag tree carries 'Scan shape X' under more than one object (e.g. a 256-wide survey beside a 64x32 acquisition). `scanShape("Scan shape X")` returns whichever the dictionary happens to yield, so the frame series is folded as 32 rows x 64 columns on one launch and 64 x 32 on another. Both pass the byte-count check, both open without error, and every scan-indexed product — virtual image, DPC, strain, ACOM map — is transposed relative to the sample on one of the two runs.

findings.title: The sidecar writer silently drops per-position origin maps it considers inconsistent, where the export path refuses on the same condition
findings.why: `writeCalibration` computes `validMaps` with a `flatMap` returning nil on a shape/count disagreement (1809-1815), then writes `qx0`/`qy0` only `if let maps = validMaps` (1830) while still writing `qx0_mean`/`qy0_mean` from whatever is available (1816-1829). A mismatch therefore produces a sidecar carrying a scalar mean and no maps, with no thrown error and no status line — the session is saved 'successfully'. The same writer's export path refuses loudly in the identical situation: `transformedCalibration` throws `invalidDimensions` with a sentence naming both shapes (1291-1298), on the stated grounds that 'there is no honest way to export them'. `ResultExport.sessionPixelCalibration:1347-1358` has a third copy of the same guard, also silent — the maps are simply omitted from the snapshot if `maps.width != descriptor.rx`. A demotion from `.sessionMaps` to `.sessionMean` on reload is a real loss of scientific content (per-position descan correction versus a single mean), and it is the one path of the three that says nothing.
findings.failureScenario: Any state in which `calibration.origin`'s extent and the descriptor's scan extent disagree — a future crop path that re-fits before the descriptor is updated, or a reload ordering bug — produces a Save Session Sidecar that reports success while writing only `qx0_mean`/`qy0_mean`. On reopen `originProvenance` becomes `.sessionMean`, `calibration.origin` is nil, and every analysis re-centres on a single mean instead of the fitted per-position map, with the inspector showing a plausible origin and no indication that the map was ever there.

findings.title: In log display, non-finite CBED pixels are mapped to 0 and then colormapped as valid data, contradicting the masked-value contract stated 45 lines above
findings.why: `FloatImage.invalidDisplayValue` and `normalized` (DiffractionPattern.swift:23-46) establish the contract explicitly: 'Non-finite pixels map to `invalidDisplayValue`, never to a valid color — "no data" must stay distinguishable from any real value', and the Metal fragment shader and PNG colormap render negatives as an explicit masked colour. `DiffractionPattern.contrastPixels(useLog:)` at :71-76 breaks it before `normalized` can see it: `$0.isFinite ? log10(1 + max($0,0)) : 0`. The NaN is replaced by a finite 0 that is indistinguishable from a genuine zero-count pixel, so `normalized` (called at :65-67) sees only finite values and emits a valid colormap entry. The linear branch at :72 passes the NaN through and the contract holds there — so the same dead pixel is masked in linear display and painted as minimum intensity in log display, which is the default for CBED.
findings.failureScenario: A detector with dead pixels, or a pattern produced by a dark-reference division that yields NaN, is viewed with log display on. The dead pixels render as the colormap's lowest colour, identical to a genuinely unilluminated region of the detector, and the histogram/contrast axis includes them as real zero-intensity samples. Switching to linear display makes the same pixels appear in the explicit masked colour — the same data telling the viewer two different things about where the detector has no measurement.
